title: Google Messages just made it easier to spot AI-edited photos in your group chats

body: TL;DR Google Messages now supports Content Credentials, letting you check how compatible photos, videos, and audio were created or edited, including whether AI tools were involved. It won’t tell you whether something is real or fake. Content Credentials only show the history attached to a file, and media without credentials won’t provide this information. The feature is currently Android-only. Press and hold supported media, tap Info, and look for How this was made to see its origin and editing history. A couple of months ago, we spotted Google Messages preparing a useful new trick for the age of AI: a way to tell you about where the photos, videos, and audio people send you actually came from. That feature is now available , and it could come in handy the next time something in your group chat looks too good to be true. Google Messages now supports Content Credentials, which essentially give compatible media a digital history. Instead of leaving you to stare at a suspicious photo and wonder whether it was shot with a camera, heavily edited, or created with the help of AI, Messages can show you some of that information directly.

body: NASA/Clayton Rougelot On Aug. 24, technicians at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began installing the four RS‑25 engines in the core stage of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that will carry the Artemis III crew into low Earth orbit in 2027. Each RS‑25 engine has a unique serial number that records its detailed flight history. The four engines assigned to Artemis III — E2054, E2057, E2048, and E2052 — previously powered multiple space shuttle missions. Engine 2048 helped launch NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik’s earlier mission aboard space shuttle Atlantis during STS‑129. It also flew on Space Shuttle Discovery during STS‑95 in 1998, the mission that returned 77-year‑old space pioneer U.S. Sen. John Glenn to orbit, making him the oldest person to fly in space at that time.

title: Pixel 11’s big modem switch hasn’t ended familiar connectivity complaints
summary: Early owners report Wi-Fi, 5G and Bluetooth problems.
body: TL;DR Some Pixel 11 owners are reporting connectivity problems, including unreliable 5G/mobile data, Wi-Fi dropouts, and Bluetooth issues. The reports are limited to a small number of users, with plenty of Pixel 11 owners saying their connectivity is working perfectly. It’s too early to blame the new MediaTek modem, as carriers, network conditions, routers, firmware, and individual hardware could all be factors. Google’s switch from Samsung Exynos to a MediaTek modem on the Pixel 11 series was supposed to close one of the longest-running chapters in Pixel history. After years of complaints around reception, connectivity, and cellular battery drain, the new modem arrived as one of the generation’s most meaningful upgrades. But just weeks after the Pixel 11 series went on sale, some owners are reporting connectivity problems that sound uncomfortably familiar.
